title: Ofe Nsala with Utazi
author: Chioma Adeleke
desc: The short version — one big catfish, eight small pieces of white yam, five utazi leaves — done when the pounded yam dissolves to a medium consistency.
longDesc: This is nsala stripped to its essentials and it is described by its own source as the quickest and easiest Igbo soup to prepare. One catfish, eight small pieces of white yam boiled until they soften and go moist then pounded until smooth and stretchy, five utazi leaves, a handful of crayfish, a small piece of ogiri okpei and habanero to taste. The yam goes into the pot in small lumps and the soup is ready when they have dissolved and it has reached a medium consistency. There is no palm oil, which is what keeps it white.
steps: Clean the catfish, cutting it into steaks, and set aside.
Boil the white yam pieces until the yam softens and becomes moist.
Pound the cooked yam in a mortar till smooth and stretchy.
Cook the catfish with the seasoning cubes, crayfish, ogiri okpei and habanero pepper.
Add the pounded yam into the pot of soup in small lumps.
Cook until the yam dissolves and the soup achieves a medium consistency.
Add the utazi leaves, taste, and add salt if necessary.
chefTips: Small lumps, not one mass. The yam dissolves from the surface inwards and small pieces get there much faster.
Softens and becomes moist is the boiling cue for the yam, and smooth and stretchy is the pounding cue. Both are worth watching for.
Five utazi leaves is a small number on purpose. Utazi is bitter and is used sparingly — one named reference calls it an excellent garnish used in small quantities.
No palm oil. Nothing that would colour the soup goes anywhere near it.
Cut the catfish into steaks rather than small chunks. It holds together better and it is how the dish is served.
This version has no stockfish and no smoked fish, so it is genuinely fast — about an hour from a standing start.
No alternative thickener is mentioned on this page at all. If you have no yam, the fuller version offers achi, yam flour or cocoyam (NGA048).
commonMistakes: Adding the pounded yam as a single ball.
Using more utazi than the five leaves, which turns it harshly bitter.
Under-pounding the yam so it stays lumpy.
Boiling hard once the catfish is in.
sources: Adapted from 'Ofe Nsala', All Nigerian Recipes — no byline on the page, credited to the site. Quantities as printed: 1 big Catfish; 8 small pieces white yam; 5 Utazi leaves; 2 small seasoning cubes; Small piece of ogiri okpei; A handful crayfish; Habanero pepper to taste; Salt if necessary.

Cues as printed: the yam 'softens and becomes moist'; pound 'till smooth and stretchy'; done when the yam 'dissolves and achieves medium consistency'. Yield not specified, so the serving figure here is a serving suggestion.
Its headnote claim, as printed: this is 'the quickest and easiest Igbo Soup to prepare.'

ON THE THICKENER: this page uses white yam and mentions NO alternative thickener anywhere. Together with Sisi Jemimah's version (NGA048) and 1Q Food Platter's Efik afia efere (NGA067), that makes three sources for this soup family, all using yam and none using ofor.

ON UTAZI, from 'African Vegetables (Leafy Greens)', byline Tayo Oredola, Low Carb Africa: utazi is Gongronema latifolium, 'Utazi/Otazi (Igbo) and Arokeke (Yoruba)', 'this lovely heart-shaped leaf with a slightly bitter taste' is 'the primary ingredient used to make Nsala soup and Utazi soup', and critically — 'Used in small quantities, these leaves serve as an excellent garnish.' That is corroborated by nkwobi and isi ewu, where utazi is garnish only.

A NAMING TRAP worth flagging: utazi, ukazi or okazi, and uziza are three different plants with confusingly similar names — Gongronema latifolium, Gnetum africanum and Piper guineense respectively. The confusion is common enough to have generated corrective articles.
reheating: Low heat with a little water.
healthBenefits: No palm oil, so much lower in fat than most Nigerian soups.
Catfish is a lean source of protein and omega-3 fats.
Utazi is traditionally used for digestion and blood sugar.
culturalNote: That the simplest Igbo soup is also one of the most prized says something about how the repertoire works: nsala has no palm oil, no egusi, no ogbono and no long list of leaves, and it is still a soup you would serve a guest. The catfish carries it, and the three dried spices do the rest.
